items.answer:
Here’s how the assistant should handle any sensitive workplace complaint and the related HR case, grounded in policy:

- Recognize what counts as “sensitive.” Treat harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats/violence, serious misconduct, medical matters, or material safety risks as sensitive issues that require human review [HR-POL-011 §3.4; HR-POL-013 §4.3].
- Prioritize immediate safety. If there’s any risk of harm, surface emergency resources and safety steps first before administrative actions [HR-POL-011 §8].
- Escalate promptly to People and Culture (HR). Do not attempt to resolve or informally investigate in chat; route the concern through the formal channel for human handling [HR-POL-011 §8; HR-POL-001 §4.2].
- Maintain confidentiality and need-to-know limits. Share details only with appropriate HR channels; avoid broad disclosure and protect any medical or highly sensitive information [HR-POL-011 §5.4; HR-POL-001 §4.2; HR-POL-013 §4.3].
- Preserve relevant information. Encourage saving any messages, dates, or artifacts without coaching or pressuring the reporter; avoid creating informal records that could compromise privacy [HR-POL-011 §5.4].
- Avoid promises or determinations. Do not decide who is right, assign fault, diagnose, or promise outcomes or specific remedies; these matters require human review [HR-POL-011 §8; HR-POL-011 §10.2; HR-POL-013 §4.3].
- Guard against retaliation. Remind managers and parties that good-faith reports must not result in adverse changes to work or any form of retaliation [HR-POL-011 §8; HR-POL-011 §5.4].
- Model respectful, neutral support. Listen, acknowledge, keep the discussion professional, and avoid pressuring the reporter to confront anyone or to provide more than the minimum needed to route the case to HR [HR-POL-011 §5.4; HR-POL-001 §4.2].

If you’re raising a concern now, I can help you route it to People and Culture and draft a note summarizing only what you want them to know while keeping details minimal and confidential [HR-POL-001 §4.2; HR-POL-011 §5.4].

citations.snippet:
All workers must contribute to a respectful, inclusive, and safe workplace.

All workers must protect confidential information and use company systems only for authorised purposes.

Concerns involving harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats, or significant security risk must be escalated through the appropriate formal channel.
citations.title: Employee Handbook

citations.snippet:
- If a concern involves harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats, or violence, escalate to People and Culture.
- Do not adjudicate a sensitive workplace issue through automated guidance.
- If immediate safety is at risk, prioritise safety and emergency support before administrative steps.
- If a person raises a concern in good faith, managers must not retaliate.
citations.title: Workplace Conduct Policy

citations.snippet:
Harassment, discrimination, retaliation, medical, safety, and other sensitive matters must be routed for human review.

The system must not determine credibility, legal liability, diagnosis, or disciplinary outcome.
citations.title: HR Requests and Case Management Procedure

citations.snippet:
A manager receiving a concern should listen, avoid promising a particular outcome, check immediate safety, preserve relevant information, and contact People and Culture. The manager should not conduct an informal interrogation or pressure the person to confront another worker.

The manager must avoid discussing the concern with people who do not need the information and must not change the person's work adversely because the concern was raised.
citations.title: Workplace Conduct Policy

citations.snippet: No. Sensitive workplace matters require human review.

Here’s what I found for E006 (Riley Chen):

- PTO balance on file: None. The system has no PTO balance record for you.
- Policy: Contractors do not accrue company PTO unless a written contract expressly grants an equivalent/named paid leave benefit [HR-POL-002 §2. Scope], [HR-POL-007 §4.1 Eligibility by employment type; §2. Scope].

What this means: If your contract does not specifically include paid leave, you won’t have company PTO. If your contract does include a paid leave provision, HR can set up the corresponding balance.

Would you like me to draft an email to HR to confirm whether your contract includes paid leave and, if so, have them add the balance?

sources.snippet:
Part-time employees receive a pro-rata entitlement based on their recorded full-time-equivalent fraction.

A change in scheduled hours applies prospectively and must not be used to retrospectively recalculate leave already taken.
sources.title: Paid Time Off Policy

sources.snippet:
Full-time employees receive 20 days of paid time off each year.

Entitlement accrues progressively across the year and is recorded in the employee's paid-time-off balance.

An employee must not represent projected future accrual as currently available leave unless the manager and People and Culture approve an advance arrangement.
sources.title: Paid Time Off Policy
